Can AI become a catalyst for sustainable development without becoming a growing burden on the planet?

That was the central question from today’s 2026 HLPF side event on Advancing Digital Environmental Sustainability for SDG Implementation. As the HLPF draws to a close, the discussion reinforced that digital transformation must be integrated into the sustainable development agenda.

AI is reshaping development, but behind every algorithm lies a physical system powered by electricity, water, minerals and infrastructure. By 2030, data centres could use 945 terawatt-hours of electricity, equivalent of the current electricity consumption of Africa.

By 2030, AI is expected to add US$15.7 trillion to the global economy, while developing countries may capture only 10% of that value.

I shared insights from UNDP ’s report, The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries, which shows that AI’s next frontier will depend as much on energy systems as computing power. It calls for Green AI that advances people, protects the planet and expands prosperity by aligning digital investment with clean energy and national priorities.

I shared three key priorities: directing AI towards practical development challenges, building skills and innovation ecosystems that create domestic value, and embedding sustainability and accountability into investment from the outset.

Examples are emerging. In Kenya, AI-enabled energy systems are improving affordability and resilience. In Moldova, UNDP is supporting 500,000 smart meters by 2030. UNDP tools, such as the Clean Energy Equity Index and the Electricity Access Forecasting Model, are helping countries improve AI and digital planning and resilience.

My takeaway is that the Global Digital Compact must move from ambition to implementation. Beyond 2030, digital progress should be defined not by technological scale alone, but by its contribution to inclusion, resilience and sustainable development.
